problem: Socially aware robot navigation research is spread across mobile robots, autonomous vehicles and drones. Earlier surveys each covered one robot type or one challenge axis: planning, conflicts, evaluation or proxemics. None gave a multi-dimensional classification that also covers environmental and task context, human-intention detection, and how specific robot characteristics shape navigation.
motivation: Delivery, assistive and service robots, autonomous cars and drones increasingly share space with people. Social acceptability, comfort and safety are therefore prerequisites for deployment. Publication counts in IEEE Xplore grew roughly exponentially over the preceding 6 years, and the fragmented literature makes it hard for developers, application designers and evaluators to find relevant work or compare methods.
key_idea: The paper organises about 10 years of socially aware navigation literature (193 articles, 2012–2022) into four orthogonal faceted taxonomies: robot type, planning and decision-making, situation awareness and assessment, and evaluation and tools. It uses deductive thematic analysis to tag every paper, then derives open research proposals and future challenges from the gaps it finds.
insight: Tagging each paper along several non-overlapping facets shows where the field is thin. Of 156 robot-tagged papers, 116 use mobile robots, 22 autonomous vehicles and 18 aerial robots; none use aquatic robots, and legged or winged platforms are rare. Implicit/explicit communication, negotiation and robot-specific parameters (shape, size) are also under-explored. In evaluation, more than 100 papers use quantitative metrics, but most discomfort metrics still derive from Hall's proxemics, and only around 33 papers run user studies. The authors argue this, together with the lack of context-based benchmarks, makes social-awareness comparisons across methods unreliable.
method: Literature collection: queried IEEE Xplore, ACM DL and Google Scholar with ('social' OR 'human-aware') AND 'navigation' AND ('robot' OR 'autonomous vehicle' OR 'drone'), restricted to about the past 10 years since Kruse et al. (2013) covers earlier work; more than 200 papers read, 193 retained after exclusion (socially aware navigation not the core topic, or only incremental over already-covered work).

Deductive thematic analysis: predefined taxonomy trees act as themes and node tags act as codes; each paper was summarised and multi-tagged over several passes, with taxonomy revisions and re-tagging.

Robot-type taxonomy: Ground (mobile wheeled/legged; autonomous vehicles incl. personal mobility vehicles), Aerial (rotorcraft, aerostat, fixed-wing, flapping-wing), Aquatic; leaf facets are mostly mutually exclusive.

Planning & decision-making taxonomy: Communication (implicit/explicit/both), type of navigation task (independent/assistive/collaborative), Negotiation, Local motion generation (planning, e.g. DWA/MPC/elastic bands; force, e.g. social force model/potential fields; learning; others), and Global motion decision-making (planning/learning).

Situation awareness & assessment taxonomy (following Endsley's definition): Environment (semantics, object interactions, obstacles), Agents (trajectory prediction, interactions & actions, intentions), and Social norms (proxemics, other conventions such as side-of-walking).

Evaluation & tools taxonomy: Methods (qualitative/subjective such as Godspeed questionnaires with ANOVA; quantitative with navigation, discomfort and naturalness metrics, summarised in Table 1) and Tools (simulators, datasets, studies, metrics & benchmarks, e.g. SEAN, SocNavBench, SocialGym, THÖR, SCAND, SocNav1/2).

Synthesis: eight research proposals (e.g. richer human models, user-adaptive behaviour, context-based benchmarks, robot-specific parameters, communication protocols, alternatives to proxemics metrics, comfort/trust, dynamics of fast agents) plus long-term challenges covering culture, urban design, regulation, AI and evaluation.

setting.simulator: n/a (reviews simulators such as SEAN / SEAN 2.0, SocNavBench, SocialGym, HuNavSim, Pedsim/ORCA-based tools)

numbers_note: Survey paper; it reports no experimental benchmark results. The only counts are about the literature: 193 articles analysed; of 156 robot-tagged papers, 116 mobile robots, 22 autonomous vehicles and 18 aerial robots; 149 methodological papers mapped to the planning taxonomy; more than 100 with quantitative evaluation; around 33 with user studies. The middle portion of the text (sections 4–6 body) was trimmed in the provided source.
results: This is a taxonomic survey of 193 papers, not an experimental paper. Most socially aware navigation work targets wheeled mobile robots (116 of 156 robot-tagged papers). Autonomous vehicles (22) and drones (18) are emerging, and there are no aquatic works. Evaluation relies heavily on proxemics-based discomfort metrics and non-standardised custom metrics, with few user studies (around 33). The authors conclude that context-aware benchmarks, better human models (intentions, reactions) and robot-specific and communication-aware designs are the main open needs.
limitations: Qualitative taxonomic review with no quantitative meta-analysis or head-to-head comparison of methods; the classification is subjective, based on the authors' tagging.

Coverage is skewed toward mobile robots and limited to roughly 2012–2022. Exclusion of 'incremental' works may omit relevant papers, and embodied-AI simulator-based social navigation (e.g. Habitat-style benchmarks) is barely covered.
Aquatic robots and winged drones get essentially no analysis because of scarce literature.
